claim: This type is a chain of four fixed filter sections and an output gain: a low shelf, two peaking sections that share one law, a high shelf. The low shelf is one pole and one zero, and so is the high one -- which the band profiles this was read from could not say, because they are magnitude and a second-order section differs from a first-order one in phase everywhere and in magnitude only past a corner this unit has no output beyond. Each parameter byte selects from a short table rather than driving a formula -- a gain answers over twenty-five values and sticks at both ends, a corner has two states, a width has five entries and returns the first for anything past them, a centre moves in equal steps of log frequency for every eighth value of its byte, at the named third octaves between the printed ends and at one entry that is not one of them.
whyNotNamed: Naming it would add nothing the claim does not already say and would carry a topology this run did not test. The high shelf's order is open, and a name would close it by implication.
adds: The archive says what each byte did to each band. It does not say that those profiles are the response of a cascade of second-order sections, that the low shelf is one pole rather than two, or that the two mids are one law rather than two that happen to agree at the three settings both were asked at. Each of those is a structure fitted to the readings, and the fit is what this file holds.
refutedBy: A setting of any of the eleven bytes whose band profile the chain cannot produce at all -- a second peak, an asymmetric one, a corner that moves with the gain applied through it. Or a byte turning out to answer at values the tables here say are repeats: the widths at 5 and above, the centres between multiples of eight, the gains outside 52 to 76.

eraPriors.claim: A parameter byte indexes a coefficient table rather than driving a formula.
eraPriors.why: Computing a filter coefficient from a byte needs transcendental functions a fixed-point part of that period does not have, and a table of a few tens of entries costs it nothing.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: A parameter answered differently at every one of its 128 values with no repeats. Four of this type's eleven bytes repeat: the widths have five entries, the corners two, the centres one per eight values, and the gains one per value over a window of twenty-five.

eraPriors.claim: The chain runs below the converter's rate, so its response ends at that rate's half.
eraPriors.why: Effect processing shared a slower clock than the output in this generation of part.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: The unit answered above the half rate the model assumes. It does not: the output stands 31.9 dB over silence at 16 kHz, 16.3 at 17 and nothing at 18.

alternatives.reading: The high shelf is one pole and one zero, as the low one is.

separatedBy.observable: The high shelf's profile where it levels off.

predicts.first order: About 3.6 dB per octave through the corner.

separatedBy.sensitivity_here: The slope is published at two resolutions and they agree for the low shelf (3.5 to 3.7) and disagree for the high one (7.1 against 9.8), which is what a profile still climbing at the edge of the set does.
separatedBy.why_not_separable: Superseded, and kept because the reason it gave is worth reading against what happened. It was right that the profile does not level off before this unit's output ends and right that no stimulus can be put past it. Its last sentence -- that no further reading of these takes would separate the two -- was written when the only reading there was read band energy, and it did not hold: the takes had phase in them all along.

alternatives.reading: The low shelf is a second-order shelving section.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: Its residual leans across the bands of the low corner's record where the first-order one does not, and the low shelf's profile did settle inside the band set, so the lean is the model's and not the reading's. The two candidates that put a second-order section at the low end are the only two of the five that lean on a record whose profile the bands contained.

alternatives.reading: The width byte selects the Q values the manual prints against it.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: It leans on 11 of the 22 records that carry an effect, against none for the winner, and its residual is the largest of the eight candidates on every record that carries one. Since this was first written the width byte has a class of its own and the printed figures were scored against every record of this type that sweeps one: they give seven times the winner's residual there and are refuted by the width the unit puts over half its peak, which is forty-nine bands where the printed figures render thirty.

alternatives.reading: The third entry of the centre table is a third octave like the other fifteen, and what the runs read there is something about the reading rather than about the table.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The chain carrying 315 Hz there breaks down at the setting that selects it -- 6.57 dB, a share of 0.527 of that record's span -- and every record whose residual leans is a record that sweeps across it. The chain carrying 279 does neither, and the two differ in nothing else. The entry is two bands of this reading below the series against the half band it resolves, five settings across the type's two mid addresses return it, and the same section inside two combination types returns it as well. What is not settled is why, and that is a different sentence.

#include <cmath>

namespace soundings::roland_sc8850_01::type_01_00 {

// The unit's own output ends between sixteen and eighteen kilohertz, measured: thirty-two
// decibels over silence at sixteen, sixteen at seventeen, nothing at eighteen. A chain
// running at thirty-two kilohertz ends exactly there. The rate is part of the candidate
// rather than a constant, so a reading above the half-rate is dropped by name instead of
// being answered with a number the model never said.
constexpr double kSampleRateHz = 32000.0;
constexpr double kPi = 3.14159265358979323846;

/**
 * A first-order shelf: one pole, one zero, tilting the two sides of its corner
 * against each other. `(s + w0 * V) / (s + w0)` for a low shelf and
 * `(V * s + w0) / (s + w0)` for a high one, bilinear-transformed.
 */
struct Shelf1 {
  enum class Side { Low, High };

  double b0 = 1.0, b1 = 0.0, a1 = 0.0, x1 = 0.0, y1 = 0.0;

  void set(double hz, double gainDb, Side side) {
    const double v = std::pow(10.0, gainDb / 20.0);
    const double k = std::tan(kPi * hz / kSampleRateHz);
    const double norm = 1.0 / (1.0 + k);
    a1 = (k - 1.0) * norm;
    if (side == Side::Low) {
      b0 = (1.0 + v * k) * norm;
      b1 = (v * k - 1.0) * norm;
    } else {
      b0 = (v + k) * norm;
      b1 = (k - v) * norm;
    }
  }

  double process(double x) {
    const double y = b0 * x + b1 * x1 - a1 * y1;
    x1 = x;
    y1 = y;
    return y;
  }
};

/** A second-order section, set the way the audio cookbook sets one. */
struct Biquad {
  enum class Side { Low, High };

  double b0 = 1.0, b1 = 0.0, b2 = 0.0, a1 = 0.0, a2 = 0.0;
  double x1 = 0.0, x2 = 0.0, y1 = 0.0, y2 = 0.0;

  void setShelf(double hz, double gainDb, Side side) {
    const double a = std::pow(10.0, gainDb / 40.0);
    const double w = 2.0 * kPi * hz / kSampleRateHz;
    const double cs = std::cos(w);
    // Unit slope, which is what `order 2` means here.
    const double alpha = std::sin(w) / 2.0 * std::sqrt(2.0);
    const double two = 2.0 * std::sqrt(a) * alpha;
    const double sign = side == Side::Low ? 1.0 : -1.0;
    const double a0 = (a + 1.0) - sign * (a - 1.0) * cs + two;
    b0 = a * ((a + 1.0) + sign * (a - 1.0) * cs + two) / a0;
    b1 = sign * 2.0 * a * ((a - 1.0) + sign * (a + 1.0) * cs) / a0;
    b2 = a * ((a + 1.0) + sign * (a - 1.0) * cs - two) / a0;
    a1 = -sign * 2.0 * ((a - 1.0) - sign * (a + 1.0) * cs) / a0;
    a2 = ((a + 1.0) - sign * (a - 1.0) * cs - two) / a0;
  }

    const double a = std::pow(10.0, gainDb / 40.0);
    const double w = 2.0 * kPi * hz / kSampleRateHz;
    const double alpha = std::sin(w) / (2.0 * q);
    const double a0 = 1.0 + alpha / a;
    b0 = (1.0 + alpha * a) / a0;
    b1 = -2.0 * std::cos(w) / a0;
    b2 = (1.0 - alpha * a) / a0;
    a1 = b1;
    a2 = (1.0 - alpha / a) / a0;
  }

  double process(double x) {
    const double y = b0 * x + b1 * x1 + b2 * x2 - a1 * y1 - a2 * y2;
    x2 = x1;
    x1 = x;
    y2 = y1;
    y1 = y;
    return y;
  }
};

extra.key: why this is not a round
extra.text: `rounds` counts revisions of a claim's model, and this model file is unchanged: the same four sections, the same corners, the same tables and the same orders. What was revised is the code that renders it and the set of things the archive can read, and the alternative the wave settled is this claim's own reading of the high shelf rather than a rival to it -- taking it up swaps no model for another. The claim is at its ceiling of three and parking it here would file a claim that has just lost its last open reading as one still waiting on something.
